A new site design and wordmark for Hyperallergic’s next era.

From the start in 2009, Hyperallergic has been kicking at the doors of the art world status quo, challenging assumptions about what is worthy of investigation and investment, and the supposed neutrality of those decisions. Today, 17 years later, we are no longer a young upstart blogazine but a daily source of trusted news, reviews, and opinions for millions in the art community.

We’ve transformed our strategy for sustainable revenue and evolved our editorial approach several times over the years to meet the unique challenges of each internet era. While so many of our peers have disappeared, we’ve survived as an independent media company throughout it all. It’s never been easy, but it’s always been worth it.

As we enter yet another new era, with social media becoming ever more toxic and AI seemingly overtaking every aspect of our lives, we want to refocus ourselves on being the best place for our community to gather. For all of us to learn, to grow, to laugh, and to feel connected to each other.
Today, we are excited to introduce the next transformation of this site, with a whole new look, a dynamic homepage, and the third version of our wordmark.

It’s clear that the insistent and demanding bright cyan of the site is no longer needed, and it is time for Hyperallergic to look more like the authoritative publication it has now become. (And for those who always loved the blue, you’ll see it re-emerge in spots over time.)

The Brooklyn-based design cooperative, Partner & Partners , has created a warm and inviting new look and organizational framework that fits our evolving output and will help us expand into the future.

Our new wordmark is drawn from Hyperallergic TwoOneFive, a new custom typeface made for us by Commercial Type . It is a grotesque that harkens back to the days of the Bauhaus and is full of unique quirks that push it into the future. Letting go of the uppercase blue condensed wordmark, the new logotype leans towards classic while remaining full of energy. The high bar of the capital H leads us into the lowercase title; this itself is a marker that we no longer need the screech of all caps.

Hyperallergic is by and for art-focused readers and writers, so the site has to encourage both. Spectator, a new serif typeface also from Commercial Type, brings a richness and warmth to the screen. Compared with more traditional typefaces, Spectator is clean with soft corners and is bolder all around, encouraging the eye to move from line to line.
We’re foregrounding our authors' names to highlight our team and many guest contributors, and the effort and care that goes into all the work you see on the site.

With a vast archive of tens of thousands of posts from thousands of writers and spanning nearly two decades, we’ve built a whole new search experience and a reorganized tagging system to allow readers to discover connections between writers, themes, and subjects that might otherwise get lost.
This new site design allows for more diversity in article layouts and lets us give prominence on our homepage to stories we think deserve more of your attention.

But ultimately, one of the design’s strongest elements is its ability to get out of the way. While vastly improving the user experience, it rarely draws attention to itself, instead allowing the focus to be on the content of the site, rather than the frame.

This redesign is just one part of a bigger shift. You may have noticed we now ask you to sign in to a free account to read most articles. That’s because we want to build a closer relationship with our readers and a more sustainable platform to publish the news, reviews, and commentary that keep you engaged, informed, inspired, and entertained. All while speaking truth and challenging the status quo in the art world.

Open-source tools like Ghost allow us to remain insulated from the whims of platforms funded by venture capital, with sky-high investments and unrealistic valuations that inevitably force them to pivot or shut down. Tools like these have allowed us to keep publishing without fear for the past 17 years and invest in what matters most: connecting our writers to our readers.

Visa has a new look by Base Design. So what’s actually changed?
The payment giant has had its first significant refresh since 2021, yet its famous wordmark hasn’t changed. So what’s new? And how far can a studio nudge a legendary brand that billions of…

The payment giant has had its first significant refresh since 2021, yet its famous wordmark hasn’t changed. So what’s new? And how far can a studio nudge a legendary brand that billions of people already know by heart? We find out.

It’s one of those logos you see pretty much every day but don’t think much about. Perhaps it’s because it means we’re about to spend some hard-earned cash. Or maybe we just don’t care. But you’ll know the Visa logo when it’s mentioned. It’ll flash up in your head as familiar as the faces of the people you love. So when you look at Base Design’s new identity for the brand, can you spot the difference?

That’s what I find most fascinating about a job like this. When a logo is so famous and features on a zillion cards and on shop doors all over the world, how much room does a design studio really have to play with? You certainly can’t rip it up and you can barely touch it. Yet Visa wanted to feel fresh for a new generation of spenders, so something had to give.

“When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn’t recognition. It’s relevance,” says Min Lew, managing partner and executive creative director at Base Design. “Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the net generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”

So what has changed? Three things, apparently. Base worked on the overhaul with Visa’s in-house studio to create a new symbol, a graphic device and a typeface. What’s interesting is that every one of them is borrowed from something Visa already owned.

The symbol, for example, is a ‘V’ lifted straight from the wordmark and it still has the little wingtip on its corner. This will begin to appear on some cards and across Visa’s digital assets, where four letters can prove to be a squeeze. Base stresses that it doesn’t replace the wordmark we all know and always appears alongside it. What it has ditched is the blue, white and yellow flag symbol that was introduced in 2021.

The typeface, Visa Sans, was created by Displaay Type Foundry and takes inspiration from the wordmark, too. It’s geometric for consistency at every scale, and its rounded forms hope to warm things up.

Then there’s the “hero graphic device”, a phrase coined by Base. It’s a bar, derived from the bands of the original Visa logo. Which sets us up nicely for a history lesson: when Bank of America launched BankAmericard in 1958, the name sat between a blue band and a gold one, and those bands stayed put when the card became Visa in 1976. They disappeared in the mid-2000s, leaving the wordmark to breathe on its own. Now those bands are back, sort of, as a single bar that can hold the wordmark, ‘V’ symbol or a message.

It’s only a tiny change but graphic designers will see it as the boldest. The wordmark can now be cropped at the bar’s right-hand edge, so ‘Visa’ runs off the side as if it’s pulling everything forward. It’s what Kellogg’s has done for ages, showing just a hint of the full wordmark and yet we all know exactly what it is.

“The most powerful identities are built on simple ideas with extraordinary depth,” adds Lew. “More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity. This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences. Each expression is distinct, yet unmistakably Visa.”
How far is far enough, though?

It’s worth taking notes from Visa’s last brand refresh. In 2021, Mucho redrew the wordmark, brightened the blue and then split the tricolour symbol off as an asset in its own right. Five years on and that symbol is being retired, yes, but Mucho’s wordmark has become the source material for everything else.
On asked how far it could go, Base seems to have said, backwards. It’s dipped into the archive and found something meaningful in the four letters themselves.

It’s not every day that one of the most influential graphic designers of the last five decades changes jobs, but Neville Brody has done just that, making November quite the surprise.

Reading through everything else this month, it’s clear design is playing a much bigger role across the board. Apple’s agency, TBWA\Media Arts Lab, has never had a global chief design officer before, and now it does. Brody says he’s moved to Toaster so that brand thinking is right there from the beginning, not some kind of afterthought. Then there’s Legora, a legal AI firm that poached someone from Uber. Landor and Design Bridge have also been busy, changing their leadership within a month of each other. And gosh, TBWA\Media Arts Lab kept popping up again and again – it’s clearly a place where the best people are trained.

Another thing that stood out was AI, which gets a mention in almost every press release we read. Mostly it’s about why human judgment matters more than ever. Meanwhile, the wins belong to the independents this month. We’ve got news of an agency less than a year old now leading creative for Hargreaves Lansdown and a whole load of news from the smaller studios, too. November, you’ve been brilliant. Here’s why.
Neville Brody takes the creative chair at Toaster

The man behind The Face has left Brody Associates to become creative chair at Toaster , the creative product marketing agency founded in 2010 by former Google creatives. It formalises a long relationship, as he was already on the board as an adviser. In his new role, he’ll work across clients and set up a lab exploring where creative meets tech, with Toaster Labs launching on his arrival. He isn’t starry-eyed about AI. The Florida studio has created a full brand universe for Vollie, a new haircare company on a mission to “Bottle the salon”.

Salon-quality haircare at home sounds fantastic, doesn’t it? For precisely this reason, though, the number of competitors in this space is enormous. So if you’re launching a new brand, how do you convince people you’re worth investing in? That was the challenge facing Yungbld , an independent, female-owned branding and design studio based in Florida, when its founder was building a haircare startup called Vollie.
Yungbld set out to strike a perfect balance between premium and approachable. No mean feat, and they didn’t stop at a logo and a label.

“The founder came to us with an idea to ‘bottle the salon’ and a formula,” explains Laura Miller, founder and creative chief at Yungblud. “And we built the brand into a full visual universe spanning strategy, identity, packaging, product design, CGI and animation, launch imagery, and an immersive digital experience at vollieverse.com.”

The new brand evolved from a clever tagline: ‘Handle With Haircare’. It’s a neat play on the warning you’d typically see on fragile parcels, and beautifully sets up the tension the brand is built on. Namely, that haircare products are meant to be gentle by design, but powerful in performance.

“We developed the entire experience around the idea ‘Handle With Haircare’, using sleek forms, dreamy textures, soft shadows and a restrained palette to create something that feels both premium and emotionally warm,” says Laura.
That restraint shows most clearly in the colour system. Yungbld has limited the palette to three pastels—candy pink, lilac, and pale periwinkle—anchored by black and a cool grey.
In one of the launch images, the studio depicts this literally as a Pantone swatch strip held over a model’s face, listing 230 C, 2635 C, 2120 C, Black 7 C and Cool Gray 2 C.

To balance all that softness, the typography is based around heavy, chunky, all-caps sans-serif. Black and bold, it’s the perfect choice for the wordmark, a series of one-word campaign posters (Oiled, Glossed, Brushed, Stacked) and crossheads on the website.
On launch, Vollie’s range features three products: Super Soft, a softening and strengthening hair mask; Dream Defender, a prepare-and-protect hair oil; and So Glazed, a resurfacing gloss.
Each gets its own pastel. All three share a cylindrical bottle with a ribbed cap and a pointed nozzle. The wordmark is moulded into the bottle in relief rather than printed.
Yungbld also designed products beyond the bottles, including a wide-tooth comb with the wordmark running down its spine and clear tinted zip pouches that show the bottles inside.

The CGI work leans into that idea of ‘dreamy textures’, with generous use of pastel soft gradients. The live-action imagery, though, takes a different route: warm, grainy and purposely lo-fi; again, achieving a lovely visual balance.
Overall, this brand launch impressed me by its heady combination of confidence and scale.

It would have been tempting to launch Vollie with a brief Instagram teaser, and a nice bottle and not much else. Instead, Yungbld has come out guns blazing, crafting a full brand world where packaging, product, motion, photography, and web all benefit from a shared language.
It’s soft where it needs to be and bold where it counts… just like the haircare products themselves.

Su Blackwell Enchants with Folkloric Stories That Spring from Vintage Books
The artist's new exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us.

From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist Su Blackwell carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptures. Her latest body of work, opening this week in a solo show titled Pathway of Crumbs , draws on fairytales and folklore, a fitting topic for such dreamlike scenes.

Nodding to the enduring children’s story of Hansel and Gretel , the exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us. “In Flight,” for example, stretches nearly 3.5 feet as a swarm of butterflies emerges from the flared pages of a book. “Break off my Branches” is similarly dynamic, with a flock of multi-colored birds perched on the spindly stems that burst from a splayed edition.

Blackwell selected this particular set of books because they’ve been in her collection for several years, allowing the artist to digest their contents and ruminate on how they might emerge over time. Some she’s left in the same condition since purchasing them from a secondhand shop, and others she’s minimally cut and spliced for earlier projects. All, though, have remained a compelling artifact of human knowledge and a collective desire to create, one she transforms anew into striking compositions at the intersection of nature and culture.
Pathway of Crumbs is on view from November 25 to January 25 at Long & Ryle in London. Find more from Blackwell on her website .

Helen Bur’s Monumental Bordeaux Mural Celebrates Motherhood and Female Solidarity, France
British street artist Helen Bur completes her largest mural to date in Bordeaux's Grand Parc neighbourhood, celebrating motherhood, female solidarity and community connection through EXIT's…

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.

Susitse’s lifelong interest in canids didn’t just push the Finnish illustrator, comic artist and graphic designer also known as Essi Välimäki to refine her creative skills. Ιt was a springboard to seek self-knowledge and perfect the art of self-expression. Her striking, colour-saturated illustrations look straight into the mouth of the beast and expose its heart — inner demons, low self-esteem, toxic relationships, overthinking, grief. A life spent on autopilot.

What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? This November 20th, GraffitiStreet Gallery presents OUTSIDE IN, a group exhibition bringing together internationally recognised artists whose practices are rooted in graffiti and street art. Exploring the journey from public space to the studio, the exhibition considers how an artist’s distinctive visual language moves between different settings, scales and materials, and how these transitions change the way we experience their work.

A graffiti tag, a mural spanning a building, a canvas contained within a frame and a sculpture within the gallery each create a different encounter with the viewer. Site can amplify or redirect meaning, scale can alter our response, and material can reveal another dimension of an artist’s practice. Yet across these shifts, the symbols, ideas and signature styles that define each artist remain unmistakable. How much of urban art is bound to its setting, and how much travels with the artist?
As the street enters the gallery, OUTSIDE IN invites visitors to discover what changes, what intensifies and what endures.

German artist Case Maclaim , a pioneer of photorealist graffiti, moves between monumental murals and intimate studio paintings, bringing the technical precision and extraordinary attention to detail that have defined his practice into a more concentrated setting.

Spanish duo PichiAvo unite classical sculpture and graffiti, bringing ancient mythology into dialogue with contemporary urban culture. Their distinctive compositions challenge the boundaries between artistic traditions, allowing the language of the street to coexist with the enduring influence of classical art.

South African artist Faith47 , internationally recognised for her poetic large-scale murals, extends her practice into sculpture, exploring how familiar themes and imagery acquire a different physical presence through material and form.

British artist My Dog Sighs transforms overlooked objects and unconventional surfaces into emotionally resonant artworks, while Sweet Toof brings the irreverence of his unmistakable teeth motif into paintings that connect graffiti, portraiture and art history.

Belgian artist Joachim Lambrechts balances spontaneous mark-making with carefully considered compositions, while South African artist Sonny Sundancer explores the expressive possibilities of abstraction beyond his large-scale street practice. Nean Kingdom , whose distinctive imagery has become an instantly recognisable part of his artistic identity, similarly demonstrates how a visual language developed through street art can retain its character in the studio.

Although their approaches differ considerably, each artist offers a perspective on the relationship between artistic identity and environment. Moving between the street and the studio becomes more than a change of location; it creates opportunities to experiment with materials, reconsider scale and develop ideas beyond the conditions in which their practices first emerged.
An Exhibition Across Materials and Disciplines

Alongside the featured artists, OUTSIDE [IN] includes selected artworks and collectables by Banksy, STIK and TOX, bringing further dimensions to the exhibition’s exploration of graffiti and street art.

From the repetition of a graffiti tag to the intimacy of a painting, the exhibition reveals how urban art continues to evolve across disciplines while retaining its connection to the visual culture of the street.

Together, these diverse practices create an opportunity to experience familiar artistic languages in an entirely different context, encouraging visitors to look beyond the surface and consider the ideas, techniques and identities that give each artist’s work its distinctive character.

JM Brea has painted La Crucifixión del Cristo de los Remedios outside the chapel of the Santísimo Cristo de los Remedios in Montehermoso, Spain. Made for the town council, the mural stops just before the first nail is driven through Christ’s hand. Brea places the moment of impending violence beside a chapel whose altar holds an image of the crucified Christ.

In Brea’s account of the composition, Christ’s hand rests against the wood of the cross while a nail is held over its palm. The action has not yet happened: the pointed nail and the waiting hand carry the tension. Brea describes the treatment as Baroque in character, a choice tied to the chapel rather than simply to the biblical subject.

The painting also draws on details at the site. Three nails represented at the top of the main altarpiece find an echo in the mural’s single poised nail and the shadow of three fingers across the painted wood, according to Brea. Outside, three granite crosses stand near the chapel. These connections give the work a particular setting: its scene begins on the exterior wall, while the crucifixion appears in the sculpture inside.

Montehermoso’s town council dates the chapel to the 16th century and describes it as regional Baroque in style. The image of the Cristo de los Remedios inside is from the 18th century. The chapel remains associated with the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and devotions to Christ of the Remedies, making Brea’s subject closely bound to the building’s use as well as its decoration.

The mural is part of Vientos del Pueblo, a literary and cultural route developed with Montehermoso’s schools and local partners. The project links artistic work in the town to education and local heritage. Brea’s contribution is grounded in one place: the chapel, its crosses and the image encountered within.

When news emerged that there would be a new adaptation of Stephen King ‘s Carrie on the way, there was immediate apprehension. Not only is the novel still highly regarded more than 50 years after its release, but we’ve gotten multiple successful adaptations of it over the years. If there was any glimmer of excitement about it, that was because Mike Flanagan was attached to it.

Having already developed adaptations of King stories like Gerald’s Game , Doctor Sleep , and The Life of Chuck , Flanagan has established himself as a talented adapter of King’s work. Ahead of its release, the filmmaker teased that the Prime Video series wouldn’t be what people were expecting, and he made good on that promise.

The ending of the original Carrie is one of the most famous in all of horror, and while the novel and previous versions end with Carrie White’s death, Flanagan instead ensured her survival, with the season finale seeing Summer H. Howell ‘s Carrie heading out on a journey to potentially meet other women with similar abilities. Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter , Flanagan broke down how he landed on this conclusion for Season 1.

“It happened organically in breaking that first season, in contemplating this very different version of who Carrie White was,” Flanagan explained. “She’s a very different character than she’s ever been. That character — starting her from a place of such kind of wide-eyed innocence and this core of her that’s so earnest and eager and kind and curious about the world. It broke my heart to imagine a version of the story that she didn’t survive .”

He continued, “The first time I came back and said, ‘Well, here’s what I see for a season of Carrie — if it were going to be a limited series, here’s how I would see it.’ Even then, it felt right to me that she survived the story and go out into the world. I thought she’d earned it. Whether we’d ever follow her into that world was the open question, but we’d see her go. That was always part of the pitch for it. It’s nice to say there’s potential in a story for the audience to get to continue on the road with the character, but it felt to me that this particular incarnation of the character — I didn’t want to live in a world where she died at the end of it .”

Ahead of the release of the first season, Flanagan teased that he had a three-season plan in mind for the series. Luckily, it didn’t take too long after the release of Season 1 for Prime Video to confirm it had renewed the show for a Season 2 .
Much like how Flanagan has hopes for Carrie, Howell herself has similar hopes for what’s in her character’s future.

“I think she ends this series off in a really dark, dark place, but at least with a little excitement to be out in the world. And I think we just, it would be cool if we could see that, see her go on an adventure, experience things,” Howell revealed to Bloody Disgusting . She joked, “I always talked about her going to the zoo. I don’t know if they’ll put that in.”

On January 22nd, 1892, Edvard Munch had a panic attack.

The esteemed artist was walking with two friends along a fjord in Oslo, Norway, before he took a moment to collect himself on the fence running between the shore and the water. He would later say that in that moment, “I sensed an infinite scream passing through nature.”

That’s a feeling that would shake anyone to their core. However, Munch at least had a way of expressing it. He turned that image into a sort of self-portrait. Putting a proxy of himself at the very centre of it, except rather than just feeling the torment within, this new version was actively vocalising what Munch felt was passing through nature. Under a blood-red and pus-yellow sky, and a river stretching out of whirling blues and whites, the subject of the painting turns to face the viewer, hands clasping their face as they let out The Scream .

It’s one of the more bizarre works of art to become as globally, undeniably famous as it is. It’s by no stretch of the imagination beautiful the way that something like Mona Lisa , Sunflowers or Girl With a Pearl Earring is. This isn’t something that makes any viewer feel good or “enriched” in the traditional sense. In fact, quite the opposite.

It’s no surprise to find that the inspiration for the work was a literal panic attack; one can feel that ineffable feeling of dread and hopelessness at its core. Yet it’s also one of the most valuable works of art ever created.

Which is truly baffling. Not because it’s not a staggering artistic achievement, but since when has the market for high art ever rewarded things for being staggering artistic achievements? It’s like if Joy Division’s ‘Atmosphere’ became one of the biggest-selling singles of all time. It’s not like it doesn’t deserve it, or that everyone hasn’t been in that kind of a dark place before, but still, works of art depicting those mental states don’t often get so ubiquitous.

In that case, perhaps its fitting that the moment The Scream became the target of one of the most infamous art heists of all time, it wasn’t in some Thomas Crown Affair style daring, style heist, but something that more resembled a mugging.

In 2004, The Scream had long been removed from the commercial sales market and was owned by the City of Oslo. It was the crown jewel of the city’s Munch Museum, and on the morning of Sunday, August 22nd, two masked men with guns burst into the gallery, making a beeline for the iconic painting.

While one of them held gallery staff and tourists alike at gunpoint, forcing them onto the floor, the other set about ripping The Scream and another Munch masterwork, titled Madonna , off the wall with his bare hands. These were clearly not criminal masterminds, as they literally dropped Madonna on the floor as they ran for the exit, but the gambit worked and two years later, the painting still remained at large.
Oslo had offered a two million kroner reward for any information that led to the painting’s recovery, but in 2006, it seemed that the deal had to be quite literally sweetened.

M&Ms were launching a new dark chocolate flavour, and for some bizarre reason, the company thought to offer a reward alongside Oslo’s financial reward. They said that whoever helped recover the painting wouldn’t just receive two million kroner, they’d also receive two million M&Ms. This put some serious egg on their face when the painting was uncovered thanks to a tip-off from a convicted criminal who revealed the painting’s location as a way of securing a lighter sentence.

Not wanting to give a metric ton of candy to a literal criminal, M&Ms changed course slightly and instead gave the monetary value of two million pieces of their candy (around 140,000 kroner) to the Munch Museum to help with its restoration.

The cruel world of Octopus Wrestling, the most bizarre sport ever which was finally banned in 1976
People really will watch anything, won't they?
One wonders what the editors of Mechanix Illustrated magazine thought when they received a pitch for an article about the writer’s sport of choice, titled ‘Octopus Wrestling is my Hobby’.

In fairness, perhaps it was because the year was 1949. Anything that could keep people’s minds off that thing that ended four years ago was worth a try. Especially considering the emergence of all the horrifying secrets the enemy was keeping. The war was over only in terms of he cessation of conflict, but the world kept going in its shadow for decades. So God help us all, sometimes we just need to stop thinking about the world and start thinking about some freak who wrestles sea creatures for his kicks.

The author wasn’t kidding either. Wilmon Menard wrote about his time in Tahiti, where he assisted local hunters in taking to the water and killing an octopus that Menard said had 25-foot-long tentacles. The absorbing way he wrote about this experience, plus his insistence that it had done amazing things for his mental and physical health, meant that the article became a sensation. So much so that diving clubs in the Pacific Northwest thought this would be a brilliant idea to adapt into a proper sport.

The first thing they did was remove the killing of it all. This wouldn’t be competitive hunting because that would be barbaric , especially considering the quarry and its rarity in parts of the ocean accessible to humans. The first version of this article adapted into a proper sport came from the Puget Mud Sharks Diving Club, where they would mark out an area between 30 and 60 feet into the sea. Then one team would dive down, coax out one of the octopuses just going about its day, then capture it and take it to land.

There, the octopus would be weighed and then released. The divers would then be given points based on the weight of their quarry, which would be doubled if they brought it to the surface without scuba gear. Other diving clubs took this rule set and began using it themselves, and suddenly, clubs would compete in octopus wrestling competitions that would attract crowds of hundreds. If you think people would just watch anything pre-TV out of boredom, you’re actually not quite right.

Perhaps it was morbid curiosity, but people tuned in to keep track of the octopus wrestling in droves. Not only as a flash-in-the-pan novelty either, but in the 1960s, there were World Octopus Wrestling Championships that attracted crowds of thousands in person and hundreds of thousands on TV. People clowned on Marty Mauser in Marty Supreme for his belief that the next big sport was ping-pong, but considering that octopus wrestling was gaining momentum at the time that film was set, maybe he had a point.

However, it couldn’t last for two reasons. For one thing, octopus wrestling was incredibly exciting… if you were 50 feet under the water where it was actually happening. Crowds in person weren’t, and TV technology of the 1960s couldn’t possibly put a camera down there. So normal people got bored of the spectacle real quick. Then the 1970s came, and the other shoe dropped. You see, by that time, the tech had been made to just about film professionally underwater, and Jacques Cousteau had used it to make Octopus, Octopus , a still astonishing documentary about how smart, gentle and all-around amazing our eight-tentacled friends are.

It was a massive hit, and suddenly, octopus wrestling began to be seen as cruel even if the quarry stayed alive after reaching the surface. Which, considering the struggle and the time out of the water, many of them did not. By 1976, the practice was banned, and while some people still try and match the glory days but doing illegal octopus wrestling bouts, they’re shamed on social media at best and arrested at worst.
Just as it should be, to be fair.

Juan Luna: The painter so evil that his paintings were thought to be cursed

It makes sense that for years, people assumed that the great work of art Portrait of a Lady by Juan Luna depicted his wife Paz Pardo de Tavera, especially if you didn’t know the full story behind their relationship.

The subject of Portrait of a Lady is bathed in almost holy white. Dressed in a white gown and relaxing on her bed, she looks at the viewer with a serene expression as she toys with a rosary that provides a spark of red across her otherwise pure chest. The soft-focus colours, teal and light orange bookending the light in the middle, the gentle line work, the overall peaceful feel of the portrait.
It makes sense that this would be how an artist would portray someone they were desperately in love with. Then you hear the other side of the story.

Juan Luna and Paz Pardo de Tavera may have been in love once, but Luna was dangerous. He had a short, easily lost temper and was violent with many people. However, he didn’t start taking that anger out on Tavera until the tragic loss of their three-year-old daughter, Maria de la Paz. Luna lost what little control he had in the aftermath of Maria’s loss. He began verbally and physically abusing her, suspecting her of having an affair and eventually beating a confession out of her at gunpoint.

Of course, there’s no actual historical record or proof that she ever had an affair. Luna was just a violent man who wanted a reason to feel like his abuse and murderous nature was justified. Paz went to her family home to hide from him to hide but it wasn’t enough. Luna broke in and shot Paz and her mother dead. Something Luna was acquitted from in 1893 by arguing that it was a “crime of passion” because of her infidelity.

It’s a testament to the sheer misogyny of the day that even Paz’s brothers testified in favour of the man who murdered their mother and sister because he told them that the woman he murdered had been unfaithful to him.

Thus, Portrait of a Lady soon became an infamous work. A woman depicted by the man who murdered her. It became such a point of conversation that people became convinced that Paz’s spirit haunted the painting. They pointed to previous owners suffering from illnesses, financial catastrophe and death, with the most famous owner being the Filipino First Lady Imelda Marcos. Supposedly, the painting hung in the Marcos residence while her family were overthrown in the People Power Revolution.

It’s a harrowing story. However, that’s all it is, for two reasons. First off, since 1986, the “cursed” painting has been housed in the National Museum of Fine Arts in Manila. 40 years on, everything has been pretty much hunky dory there. Still, that’s not the only major flaw in the story. Howie Severino made a documentary about the life of Juan Luna and, in particular, his time in Paris. While working on the documentary, he found proof that the woman in Portrait of a Lady was actually Angela Duche, a French model he often worked with.

However, this story also doesn’t really need to be “debunked” because it concerns ghosts and curses . Things that don’t exist. So, why did this story exist to begin with? Honestly, I think it’s the reason that stories develop in the first place. We see not only the horrifying end of Paz Pardo de Tavera’s life, but the knowledge that a fate like that is nowhere near as rare for women as we’d hope it to be. The injustice and the fear that reaction sparks within us are the kind we don’t process by simply talking about it, especially at the time.

People of the 1890s in Paris wouldn’t have talked about it as an injustice at all. Again, even Paz’s own brothers felt that she got what she deserved. So, how do people talk about an injustice that they can’t talk about openly? They turn it into a story. So maybe it doesn’t matter that the subject of the picture isn’t actually Paz Pardo de Tavera. If it means people remember her story and, by extension, the story of so many women whose meaningless murders people thought were justified?
Maybe that’s the very meaning of the term “print the legend.”

The Sane Out is now wherever you get your books, and it’s terrific. I’ll give a special recommendation to the audiobook, and if you haven’t seen Pen15 , you should go check it out ASAP.

What do 35 years of touring the UK look like to Manic Street Preachers?
Here’s what Nicky Wire remembers best, as told to The Quietus editor John Doran. An excerpt from issue one of SHOWNOTES.

I am very much a homebird, so when it came time for Manic Street Preachers to go on tour I was nervous about it. My Dad had an old grandad’s chair, which he managed to tie to the wall in the back of the hire van, so someone could have a seat on the way to the gig. It was incredibly dangerous. And then on the way back, James would just get in a sleeping bag and lie down in the back of the van, rolling around all over the place as we were driving back home. He can sleep anywhere.

We had such a deep bonding experience on the Motown Junk Tour in 1991. The staff at the venues were just so friendly; you felt that they really cared. I remember getting to the Stoke Wheatsheaf – a magical venue – and we hadn’t had any food for a day and a half. They made us the most beautiful burger and chips.

King Tut’s Wah Wah Hut, Glasgow? The Stoker, Coventry? The Barrel Organ, Birmingham? JB’s, Dudley? Moles, Bath? The Adelphi, Hull? The Leadmill, Sheffield? It was a truly magical tour, I can’t even remember any bad shows.

The greatest one was probably The Buzz Club in Aldershot. What a fucking venue. Who’d have thought if you were in a rock band, going to Aldershot would give you one of the greatest gigs of your life? It was full of squaddies because it’s an army town, and it was antagonistic, but also brilliant. That was on the edge but some gigs could tip over the edge.

We did quite a scary gig at Reading’s After Dark Club. There was a proper firm of football hooligans there. That film The Firm had just been on TV and I don’t know if it had got people excited but it kicked off. James got punched but we stood our ground. There was a real adrenaline rush to it, even if there was a hint of violence at a lot of those early gigs.

What strikes me now is that all of these places were towns and I wonder how many of them have that kind of gig venue left. You can still play gigs in the cities, but to play in these towns was amazing: learning your trade and meeting people. Also realising there are people like you in every town you go to.

Very early doors, Little Chefs were different – they deserve an honourable mention because you could just get a proper meal there. A plate of bacon, egg and chips. We loved going to them but even by the time we started touring they were getting harder to find. And in the services before they improved, all you could find was some dodgy pasty that had been sitting in a fridge for weeks. But I have a theory that bad food equals great music. Show me a band that’s eaten healthy food all of their lives and their music is always shit. Whereas The Fall, those bands in Seattle that just lived on hard drugs and strong coffee, Sex Pistols… they lived on bad motorway service station diets and they made the greatest music. I think if you care that much about your bodily health, you’re shutting off a pathway to creativity.

Hamburg’s Seasurfer Revisits First Love in Video for “Hush Now” — “Trip” EP Out Now!
Here we are again You look so familiar In this red light… Drop your mask, my friend Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and… The post Hamburg’s Seasurfer Revisits…

Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and bring back every little thing you did to look at ease. You remember where you put your hands and the joke you made while you worked up the nerve to ask them to stay. The relief came when they heard the question in the joke and stayed a little longer. It can take years to realize how much you miss being known that well.

At the opening of “Hush Now (The Calling),” Apolonia sings to a familiar face bathed in red light, as king them to drop the mask with the gentle insistence of an old friend inviting you to sit and stay awhile. The track is the lead single from Trip , the four-track EP released November 20 by Hamburg noise-pop trio Seasurfer .

Christian Klepp ’s footage casts the first verse’s red light across the stage. Red and yellow projections sweep the back wall, while green glints in the dark glasses above a ribbed microphone. Maysterwerke cuts from this intimate close-up to wider shots, where amber haze reduces the band to little more than silhouettes.
Watch the video for Hush Now (The Calling) below.

The way the band moves in and out of view has a counterpart in the arrangements Dirk Knight began imagining in New York. “For me, this is the sound of cities,” says the instrumentalist, who recorded, produced and mixed the EP. He keeps the bass and drums fairly still while the guitars and the voices of Apolonia and Kiora drift in and out of focus.

Those guitars have been a constant since Seasurfer’s first two albums on Saint Marie Records and through collaborations with Cocteau Twins’ Robin Guthrie and producer John Fryer. This year the band put them to work on the post-punk of June’s Angels , then let them fill the room on August’s shoegaze-heavy The Noise is ours . On their third EP of 2026, a trip-hop beat gives the guitar chords more room to ring.

You can hear that space in the first bars of the opening track , One . The guitars drone and the drums take their time, leaving room for the strings that Chandeen’s Harald Löwy adds to the arrangement. The higher voices blur into the chords the way they do on My Bloody Valentine’s Loveless . The low lead comes through with the intimacy of someone speaking in confidence. It’s a seductive way to sing about making peace with your own company and the knowledge that we come and go alone.
Watch the video for One, filmed by Ahmed Sarowar and edited by Dirk Knight, below:

That intimacy carries into Hush Now (The Calling) , where a sigh of synths stretches into long, luminous lines and Knight’s guitars bring warmth up from below. Apolonia and Kiora’s voices cascade through the chorus, opening the melody out the way Elizabeth Fraser could on Cocteau Twins’ Heaven or Las Vegas and Milk & Kisses . Apolonia describes the song as a memory of first love, and Kiora hears loss and longing in the words. When the refrain comes round to “I’m by your side,” the reassurance sounds as necessary to the person giving it as it does to the one hearing it.

The guitar comes further forward on “Disappear” , where the opening loop has the woozy repetition of Cocteau Twins’ Otherness EP. The voice has Cranes’ reserve and some of Portishead’s unease. When the drums drop away, the guitar keeps circling long enough for you to stop anticipating the next hit. By the time it comes, the loop has built up a charge that carries into the closing bars.

The drums make you wait for them again on “I See You” . The guitars pile up first, with the soft-edged distortion of Loveless , and the drum machine gives them a trip-hop lilt when it comes in. There’s some of Cranes’ distance in the singing and some of the poise of Siobhan de Maré on Mono’s “Life in Mono.” At under three minutes, the closer rewards a second pass. Follow a guitar you barely noticed the first time through, and you can hear the arrangement shift around it.

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying their miserable bills while history quietly buries the evidence. Human civilization has developed an extraordinary talent for committing atrocities, commemorating the dead, and finding fresh excuses to repeat the process. Somewhere in this grand procession of moral bankruptcy, Seattle’s Profit Prison has found sufficient inspiration to write a disco song about the unbearable weight of collective guilt.

The solo project of Parker Lautensleger, whose musical history includes Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel, and Excarnated Entity, has spent nearly a decade exploring the more psychologically disturbed possibilities of electronic pop. His latest single, In Memoriam, taken from the forthcoming album Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen? , sounds like Bronski Beat wandering into a particularly unpleasant historical reckoning, with electronic pioneer Gershon Kingsley conducting the proceedings from behind an enormous bank of synthesizers.

The arrangement possesses a strange, almost indecent sweetness. Synthesizers trace delicate melodic figures above a measured electronic rhythm, their crystalline repetitions creating the impression of a forgotten European dance record rescued from somebody’s flooded basement. Lautensleger sings with a trembling, distant resignation, his voice occupying the uncomfortable space between Neil Young’s wounded sincerity and the exquisite emotional distress of early synthpop by Das Kabinette, Depeche Mode, and others you might find on the Some Bizzare Compilation. Every syllable seems burdened by information its owner would dearly prefer to forget.

And what dreadful information it is. The lyrics describe a family whose apparently stable existence has been overturned by events unfolding near a border, where some unspecified act of violence has left questions that nobody seems willing to answer. Children inherit uncertainty, the dead receive their solemn acknowledgments, and the living are forced to contemplate the possibility that their own moral identities have been built upon carefully maintained ignorance. The song’s repeated interrogations grow increasingly desperate, suggesting a confrontation with somebody whose participation in an atrocity has become impossible to dismiss. Beneath the delicate electronic flourishes lies the hideous proposition that ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts of cruelty and subsequently spend entire lifetimes inventing explanations for themselves.

In Memoriam ‘s synthesizers maintain their patient, hypnotic progression while the words wander into the ugliest corners of human responsibility. You could conceivably dance to this record, which raises some rather uncomfortable questions about the emotional usefulness of disco. Lautensleger leaves those questions unanswered, however, allowing the music to continue its beautiful, merciless rotations while the accumulated weight of memory threatens to crush everything beneath it.

The video takes on a philosophical matter, as though we’re prisoners in Plato’s cave, watching distorted projections of events whose true nature remains somewhere beyond our comprehension. The road stretches onward, the lights assault our vision, and every image seems to conceal a fragment of some dreadful revelation.

The very British problem of GB Music Radio

How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.

My sister and I were recently hanging out at her place, and the conversation turned to our childhood. I pulled up some old photos on my phone—snaps of pictures that used to live in albums at the center of my parents’ living room. We started taking guesses about when they were from and shared stories about what was happening in them. We both remembered family picnics at the waterfall, our dog Cujo (yes, Cujo), and flying kites in the cornfield across the house. But there were people, places and stories I couldn’t recall at all, like a close family friend’s house we spent a lot of time at; my sister could still describe it in detail.
That’s when it hit me: It had been years since we’d flipped through old albums like that. As physical albums get left behind and older relatives depart, we’re increasingly losing our family history.

I’ve researched bits of my family’s genealogy over the years, but I’ve always run into roadblocks. Like many families in the U.S., our ancestors immigrated several generations ago, and a lot of details were lost or changed along the way. How do you document family history when there are so many missing pieces? By tackling it little by little, says Allison Singleton, the genealogy services manager at the Genealogy Center. “There will be gaps of information you don’t know,” she says. But don’t let that stop you.

That being said, you’ll have a lot more luck if you have a method to the madness. That’s why I reached out to a few experts who do this for a living and could lay it out in simple terms for us. In addition to Singleton, I spoke with Kyle Betit, a senior genealogist at Ancestry; Haleh Shoa, a certified professional photo organizer and the founder of Picturli; and Peter Andrew Wint, the founder of Family Roots.

It turns out, there are a lot of strategies and resources available, and some of them are free. Read on to find out how to document family history , create a family tree and be the detective your clan needs—starting now!
How on earth do you even start this kind of project?
Before you dive into documenting your family’s history, determine your goal. “Knowing where you want to end up tells you where to start and how much you need to gather,” Shoa says.

Next, collect supplies. Shoa says you’ll need several plastic bins, colorful index cards for categorizing batches of photos, an archival pencil, a 2TB or 4TB external hard drive for storage, nitrile gloves for handling photos, and a notebook or spreadsheet for tracking.

Then, gather the documentation you already have and group it into categories. Think of this like taking an inventory. “Put like with like,” Shoa says. “The albums, the slides, the negatives and the VHS tapes should each have their own piles.” In addition to photos and videos, include things like old letters , newspaper clippings, obituaries, birth and death certificates, and recipe cards. “These items are full of clues about your family history,” Singleton notes. After you’ve grouped everything, you’ll dig into each category. (More on that below.)

Keep in mind that you don’t need to do everything at once. “Start small—with one photograph, one document, one family story, one person or one question—and see how your research progresses,” Singleton advises. After all, you don’t want to get overwhelmed before you even really start!

How to Navigate Grief During the Holidays in Ways You’ll Actually Find Helpful
When the season feels anything but merry, these expert tips will give you a game plan to make it through—even when that feels impossible.

No matter what time of year you’ve lost someone, navigating that grief during the season devoted to joy, togetherness and sparkle can become a challenge unto itself. When my 82-year-old mom died the night before Thanksgiving three years ago, my grief became permanently imprinted into the holidays. Ever since, I’ve swung between wanting to eat cookies by the fire with Santa and scream through the streets with Krampus.

The holidays haven’t felt the same since, and admittedly, I even feel a little dread around this time of the year. I’m not alone. According to American Psychiatric Association’s Healthy Minds poll from 2025 about holiday-related concerns, nearly half of adults polled felt worry over grief and missing someone . The reality is that the best parts of the season can lead to some of the worst feelings of loss.

There is no easy answer here, unfortunately, but experts do have a few suggestions to help people handle grief during the holidays . For that advice, I spoke with Raman Mohabir, PhD, a licensed professional clinical counselor and the founder of Good Mourning Mental Health Counseling, and Tess Clarkson, an end-of-life doula and the creator of the Your Best Goodbye workshop.
Read on to find out how to get through the holidays after a loss , find special ways to honor your loved ones and maybe even enjoy the season again.
Why are the holidays particularly hard after a loss?

First of all, it’s not your imagination: The holidays are harder. And the first notes of a familiar holiday song or the scent of a special dish can really feel like a gut punch. “The holiday season can further magnify grief because it is a time often marked with moments meant to be spent with family and loved ones, which can further highlight the absence of the person who has died,” Mohabir says . On top of that, you may feel guilt, anger or resentment for not feeling celebratory, and your grief can feel darker against all the sparkle.

How it hits can also depend on the kind of loss. Grief isn’t only about death, Mohabir notes. It can also include “ambiguous losses, such as the anticipatory grief associated with the decline of a loved one facing a terminal diagnosis, or loss due to divorce, deployment, incarceration or a miscarriage.” Those losses can be especially lonely during the holidays. “These ambiguous and disenfranchised grief experiences can complicate the holiday season as well, especially if the loss is not acknowledged or supported by others,” she says.
Whatever kind of loss you’re carrying, feeling as if you’re living a different holiday than everyone around you can be alienating.
Should you still celebrate the holidays after a loss?

It really depends on you. “There is no correct answer or moral obligation to how an individual should navigate the holiday season,” says Mohabir. A lot of it boils down to how you feel and who will be around you . Spending time with people who share your loss, or who are simply supportive, can be a real comfort and worth the effort. Spending it with people who aren’t supportive can do more harm than good, whether they’re friends or family.

“It is important to assess the quality of the support around you and what you need when gathering with others,” Mohabir says. Time alone counts too. “Choosing solitude and privacy can be restorative and healing as well,” she adds.

If celebrating feels like too much this year, try a gentler approach: “observing” the season or focusing on getting through it rather than celebrating it. “Maybe it is not putting up the tree or getting out the menorah,” Clarkson says. It’s also not all or nothing; Show up for dessert, pop by Christmas morning—”it’s about having more serenity without the performance of the holidays,” she says.
How should you approach the holiday season after a loss?

Start by listening to yourself rather than to your list of obligations. There’s no single right way to do the holidays while grieving. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all,” Clarkson says. “It behooves us to listen to ourselves for what we need.” That might be a walk, a good cry or a quiet night in, she says, or it might be more appointments with the therapist or a grief support group.

This Junk-Drawer Staple Could Save Your Home in Case of Flooding, According to a New Study

Heavy rains and flooding are in the forecast for huge swaths of the country, leaving many wondering what they would do if water was bearing down.

Sandbags have been the go-to for centuries, but if you’ve ever tried to use them, you know they are a pain: heavy, labor-intensive and often not available when you need them. But now, researchers looking for inexpensive ways to help homeowners fight flooding have stumbled across something that blows sandbags out of the water.

Britain’s University of Hull released the surprising findings in a new report, and we have the results ahead. It turns out that something you no doubt have rattling around in your junk drawer or garage toolbox works better than sandbags—a lot better. Read on to learn an effective (and cheap) way to protect your home during a flood.
What junk-drawer staple can save your home from flooding?

That’s according to a new report called Testing the Performance of Low-cost, Temporary Property Flood Resilience (PFR) Solutions . The university teamed up with Flood Re, a partnership between the U.K. government and insurers, to pinpoint inexpensive ways for homeowners to protect their homes during a flood.

The results were amazing: Duct tape reduced water leakage 97% to 98% compared to a plain closed door. The much less common synthetic rubber tape (aka putty tape) did even better, with a 99% reduction. Even the worst-performing tape, yellow plastic tape, kept out 80% of simulated floodwaters during testing. And every single tape tested did better than sandbags, which reduced water intrusion by only 70%.

“Sandbags remain a symbol of flood protection , but these tests turn that assumption on its head,” said Jonathan Kassian, head of flood resilience at Flood Re. “What we have found is that some relatively simple and affordable products can do a much better job of keeping water out.”
Why does this work better than a sandbag?

For one thing, sandbags are porous, and they’re not designed to keep out water completely. Think of them more as a diversion tactic or obstruction, as opposed to tape, which can actually seal an opening through which water can flow.

In this study, researchers found that when placed in flood conditions of 0.2 meters (about 8 inches), sandbags leaked water at a mean rate of 584 liters per hour per meter, or 47 gallons per hour per foot. They were more effective in deeper water, but still only prevented, at most, 70% of water leakage . Sandbags are also heavy, time-intensive to deploy and difficult to place correctly.

Tape, on the other hand, is cheap and easy to store. It can be applied directly across gaps and conforms to irregular surfaces and openings where water can seep in. After the storm, cleanup is easy because tape is safely disposable, unlike sandbags, which absorb dangerous floodwater contaminants. And remember: Duct tape was more than 97% effective.
There is one caveat. Researchers concluded that how the tape was applied was “critical.” We’ll give you those details next.
How do you do this properly?

First, it’s important to understand that this was a research study about the effectiveness of certain barriers under testing conditions, not a how-to manual of using tape to stop a flood. But scientists were encouraged by the findings. Here are recommendations from the report:
Use a strong, wide tape. For duct tape, researchers recommend a width of 100 mm (roughly 4 inches).
Apply it to the flood-facing side. Tape performed best when it was applied on the outside of the door.

Cover vertical joints first. Tape the sides, making sure the vertical strip is attached to both the door and jamb and extends to the threshold. Then do the threshold and corners, overlapping the vertical strip.
Apply to clean, dry doors. To get the best adhesion, tape the door before wet weather arrives .
Make sure there are no openings. Avoid folds, press out any air bubbles and cover gaps.

Add in the rush of cold water pooling beneath her feet, and suddenly Apollon was fully alert, if disoriented. She was also fearing for her life. Actually, two lives. Apollon was in her 34th week of pregnancy on that cold morning this past February in Stuart, Florida, when she awoke to the reality that she was trapped in a sinking car .

Apollon, of nearby Port St. Lucie, had been on her way to a prenatal massage gifted by her fiancé, Woodly Sully. It was a birthday present. (Yes, this happened on Apollon’s 29th birthday.) Apollon had been struggling during her third trimester with preeclampsia, and as she drove to the massage, she began to feel woozy. She pulled her silver 2019 Hyundai Elantra over to the shoulder of Interstate 95, called Sully to let him know what was happening, drank some water, ate a little food and waited for the dizziness to subside.

After it did, about 10 minutes later, she got back on the road, but what happened next is a blur. Her car’s safety systems were beeping, telling her she was veering outside her lane, although in her haze-filled mind she was driving perfectly straight. She tried to pull over again, but started passing out. “I thought the car was in park,” Apollon recalls, “but in reality, it was still in drive.” And she drove off the right side of the road, straight into the pond.

When she came to seconds later to the sound of the splash, she unsnapped her seat belt and hit redial on her phone, then screamed to her confused fiancé, “I’m in a lake!” Within seconds, the call dropped. She and her unborn baby were all alone in a car that was listing, front driver’s side first, into a body of water.

Around this time, 29-year-old sport fisherman Logan Hayes of Sebastian, Florida, was driving down the same stretch of I-95 in his pickup, remarking to his friend and boss in the passenger seat, Chase Cornell, about how unusual it was that traffic was light and that they were running 20 minutes ahead of schedule on their work errand. “Something’s gonna happen,” Hayes joked.
Sure enough, Hayes soon saw brake lights ahead of him. And then the reason for the sudden slowdown: the Elantra, barely floating in the water.

Other cars had pulled over, but so far nobody had gotten out to help. So Hayes, also a professional surfer and confident swimmer, crossed from the far left lane across two other lanes, cutting off every car in his way, then pulled onto the shoulder and leaped out of the truck.
“Hey, is someone in that car?” he asked a bystander.

Hayes ran 50 yards down the highway, then a few more feet to the water’s edge, his eyes fixed on the Elantra. He was shedding clothing every step of the way. Off came his hat, his sunglasses, his shirt, his fishing boots, his sweatpants, his socks … until all he had on were his board shorts.

The outdoor temperature was in the mid-40s when Hayes hit the water around 8 a.m., and the pond was colder than that. But Hayes was surging with adrenaline and didn’t feel the chill as he dove in , trying to cover the distance as quickly as he could. He was underwater for a couple of seconds, then came up and took a few more strokes, and he was at the car.

With the vehicle tipping forward and to the left, the rear passenger door was the only one not submerged. Treading water, he pulled on the door handle, and it flew open. She swung her legs around so her feet were pointing toward Hayes. Now lying on her side, she pushed with her arms and slid up the console, inching toward the back seat, gravity working against her at every turn.

I hadn’t meal-prepped in months. There was a Netflix show I’d been meaning to watch, chores were piling up, and my partner and I hadn’t had much time for a quiet night together. Between work and everything else on my schedule, I was struggling to find time for much of anything.

The change in seasons wasn’t helping. By the time I finished work, it was already dark outside, and whatever motivation I had left seemed to disappear with the daylight. I was tired, had plenty to catch up on and somehow felt guilty about wanting to spend what little free time I had relaxing.

So when I came across cozymaxxing, a social media trend that encourages people to make their time at home as comfortable and enjoyable as possible, the timing couldn’t have been better. And when I learned that some of the ideas behind it overlap with an established treatment for seasonal depression, I wondered if there might be more to it than an excuse to stay home.

To find out, I spoke with a psychologist who’s spent decades researching winter depression, then gave cozymaxxing a try for three evenings. Read on to find out how my cozy little experiment went—and why you’re going to want to hop right on this cozy train.

Cozymaxxing means deliberately making your surroundings and activities as comfortable and relaxing as possible. Think: candles, blankets, warm drinks and spending an evening doing whatever sounds good to you.

The trend gained attention in 2025 through videos of cozy living-room setups, cooking, reading and movie nights. As of November 2026, more than 500 Instagram posts feature the #cozymaxxing hashtag, with some videos racking up as many as 3.4 million views.

Dictionary.com named maxxing its 2026 Word of the Year, recognizing the growing number of trends dedicated to optimizing everything from appearance (looksmaxxing) to sleep (sleepmaxxing). Cozymaxxing is a funny addition to the bunch, considering how little effort it asks of you.
Why is cozymaxxing such a good idea?
Cozymaxxing may help improve your mood by giving you something to look forward to during a season that can leave you feeling tired and unmotivated.

Kelly Rohan, PhD, a psychology professor at the University of Vermont who studies seasonal depression, says it’s common to notice changes in your mood and energy as the days get shorter. Some people barely feel the difference, while others develop seasonal affective disorder (SAD), a form of clinical depression that typically occurs during the fall and winter. Many of us fall somewhere in between, feeling more tired, sleeping longer or noticing changes in our appetite.

Shorter days appear to be a major reason why. According to the National Institute of Mental Health, people with SAD may experience changes in serotonin and melatonin, chemicals involved in regulating mood and sleep. These changes can also throw off the body’s internal clock , although researchers are still figuring out exactly how it all works.

One technique she uses is called behavioral activation, which encourages people to get out and do something they normally like, even when they aren’t feeling up to it. “Anything that one can do to approach and embrace the winter season and find some joy in it is probably going to be helpful for well-being and mental health,” she says.

Keep tabs on flammable items: Paper towels, oven mitts, wooden utensils, food packaging and curtains should stay away from hot appliances.
Establish a “safe cooking zone”: If you have children or pets, the Red Cross says to keep them at least three feet away from cooking areas.

At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for their own short adaptation of Poe’s story , which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films , you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer and B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman . Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton celebrated in animation at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe , a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on the playlist in various forms: an early D. W. Griffith feature , the directorial debut of Jules Dassin , an animated short narrated by James Mason , a British psychological thriller , and a transposition into modern-day New Orleans . And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Usher miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.
